items.prompt: What's the key difference between an example-based test and a property-based test?
choices: An example test checks one specific input against one specific expected output; a property test checks a rule that should hold for a whole class of inputs, generated automatically
A property test runs faster because it only checks one input
They are the same technique with different names
An example test can only be written for functions with no return value
items.explanation: Example tests hand-pick a specific input/output pair; property tests state an invariant that should hold across many inputs and let a tool generate those inputs, rather than a human choosing them one at a time.
items.reference:
🎯 Example — one input, one hand-picked expected output
🔁 Property — one rule, checked against many generated inputs

Why: a property doesn't need a human to imagine every input shape in advance — the generator's job is to try shapes nobody thought to write.

items.prompt: Per L1's Scenario, the encode/decode library had 6 passing example tests and still shipped a bug. What best explains why?
choices: None of the 6 hand-picked inputs happened to be an empty array — the bug only shows up on an input nobody wrote by hand
The 6 tests were run in the wrong order
JavaScript cannot represent empty arrays correctly
The tests were disabled in CI before shipping
items.explanation: Each example test only checks the specific input someone imagined ahead of time. The empty array wasn't unusual or obscure — it simply wasn't among the six inputs anyone happened to write.
items.reference:
🎯 Example — one input, one hand-picked expected output
🔁 Property — one rule, checked against many generated inputs

Why: a property doesn't need a human to imagine every input shape in advance — the generator's job is to try shapes nobody thought to write.

items.prompt: Why did generating 500 random inputs find the encode/decode bug when 6 hand-picked examples didn't?
choices: 500 random inputs cover far more of the input space than 6 human-imagined ones, including shapes a person wouldn't think to write
Random inputs are always more valid than hand-picked ones
500 is a special number that guarantees finding every bug
The generator only produces inputs known to already be broken
items.explanation: It's a matter of coverage of the input space, not magic — many more attempts, spread across many more shapes of input, greatly increase the odds of hitting the one shape that breaks the function.
items.reference:
🎯 Example — one input, one hand-picked expected output
🔁 Property — one rule, checked against many generated inputs

Why: a property doesn't need a human to imagine every input shape in advance — the generator's job is to try shapes nobody thought to write.

items.prompt: What is a "property" in property-based testing?
choices: A rule that should hold true for an entire class of inputs, not just one chosen example
A field on a JavaScript object
A single hand-picked input/output pair
A configuration setting for a test runner
items.explanation: A property is a general invariant — a true statement about the function's behavior across a whole class of inputs, not one specific case.

items.prompt: "For any string x, decode(encode(x)) equals x" is an example of what?
choices: A round-trip property
A single hard-coded example test
A test double
A mutation operator
items.explanation: This is a round-trip (inverse-function) property: doing an operation and then undoing it should return the original value, for any valid input — not just one input.

items.prompt: What does a "generator" do in property-based testing?
choices: Produces random (and edge-case-biased) test inputs of a given type, automatically
Deletes failing tests from the suite
Generates the function under test's source code
Writes the property statement itself
items.explanation: A generator's job is producing inputs — numbers, strings, arrays, custom objects — to test the property against, without a human choosing each one by hand.

items.prompt: Why do good generators deliberately produce edge cases (empty arrays, zero, negative numbers) more often than a naive uniform-random generator would?
choices: Because those are exactly the values a human writing examples by hand tends to skip, and where bugs disproportionately hide
Because edge cases are technically invalid and should be filtered out
Because it makes the test suite run faster
Because uniform-random generation is not possible in JavaScript
items.explanation: Edge cases like empty arrays and zero don't feel like 'normal' inputs to a person writing examples, which is exactly why they get skipped by hand — and exactly why generators are built to try them more often.

items.prompt: What does "shrinking" do once a property test finds a failing input?
choices: Automatically simplifies the failing input down to the smallest version that still reproduces the failure
Deletes the failing test so it stops blocking the build
Makes the generator produce smaller numbers from then on
Reruns the exact same failing input a second time to confirm it
items.explanation: Shrinking takes the first failure (which might be a large, messy random input) and tries smaller, simpler variants of it, converging on the minimal reproducing case.

items.prompt: Why is shrinking useful, rather than just reporting the first failing input a generator happens to find?
choices: A raw random failure can be large and hard to read; the minimal shrunk version is far easier to debug
Shrinking makes the property test run faster
Without shrinking, the property test could never find any bugs at all
Shrinking changes the function under test to fix the bug automatically
items.explanation: The first failure found might be a deeply nested, large random value. Shrinking turns that into the smallest input that still fails — the practical difference between 'a bug exists somewhere' and 'here is exactly what breaks it.'

items.prompt: What is a "counterexample" in property-based testing?
choices: A specific input for which the property does not hold
A test that always passes no matter what
An example test written before the property test
A generator that produces no output
items.explanation: A counterexample is a concrete input that broke the property — proof the invariant doesn't hold universally, at least not as stated.

items.prompt: A property test runs 500 times against `decode(encode(x))`, and run 340 fails on `x = []`. What is `[]` here?
choices: A counterexample — a specific input that broke the round-trip property
A generator
A mutation operator
An oracle
items.explanation: `[]` is the counterexample — the concrete input where the property ("decode(encode(x)) equals x") failed to hold.

items.prompt: What's the general lesson L1's Scenario is meant to teach?
choices: Hand-picked examples only cover the inputs someone thought to imagine; generated inputs can find real bugs no example test would ever hit
Example-based tests should never be used for anything
Property-based testing replaces the need to write any tests at all
500 is always the correct number of test runs for every function
items.explanation: The point isn't that examples are worthless — it's that a fixed, human-chosen set of examples is structurally limited to what a person thought of, and generated random inputs routinely find real bugs outside that set.

items.prompt: Per L1, is property-based testing meant to replace example-based tests entirely?
choices: No — it's a different way of generating test inputs, useful where a real invariant exists; example tests still have their place, including as a minimal regression test once a bug is found
Yes — every example test should be deleted once a property test exists
Yes, but only for functions that return numbers
No — property-based testing can only be used inside a code review, never in CI
items.explanation: Property-based testing is a complementary technique, not a replacement — it's most valuable where a genuine invariant exists to check, and a minimal counterexample often becomes a permanent example test afterward.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what kind of property is "sort(sort(list)) equals sort(list)"?
choices: Idempotence — doing the operation twice has the same effect as doing it once
Round-trip / inverse
Oracle comparison
Invariant under transformation
items.explanation: Idempotence is specifically about repeating an operation having no further effect the second time — sorting an already-sorted list changes nothing.
items.reference:
Round-tripdo A, undo A, get the original back
Idempotencedoing it twice = doing it once
Invariantsome property of the output never changes
Oraclecompare against a simpler reference implementation

Why: each pattern is a different, reusable shape for finding a true, checkable invariant — most functions fit at least one.

items.prompt: Per L2's table, what kind of property is "decode(encode(x)) equals x"?
choices: Round-trip / inverse
Idempotence
Invariant under transformation
Oracle comparison
items.explanation: Round-trip properties check that undoing an operation returns the original value — doing A (encode) then undoing A (decode) should always recover the input.
items.reference:
Round-tripdo A, undo A, get the original back
Idempotencedoing it twice = doing it once
Invariantsome property of the output never changes
Oraclecompare against a simpler reference implementation

Why: each pattern is a different, reusable shape for finding a true, checkable invariant — most functions fit at least one.

items.prompt: Checking that a fast custom sort produces the exact same output as `[...list].sort()` for every generated input is an example of which property pattern?
choices: Oracle comparison
Idempotence
Round-trip / inverse
Shrinking
items.explanation: Oracle comparison checks a function's output against a simpler, obviously-correct (even if slower) reference implementation — here, the built-in sort acts as the oracle.
items.reference:
Round-tripdo A, undo A, get the original back
Idempotencedoing it twice = doing it once
Invariantsome property of the output never changes
Oraclecompare against a simpler reference implementation

Why: each pattern is a different, reusable shape for finding a true, checkable invariant — most functions fit at least one.

items.prompt: Per L2's Checkpoint, why is "the function never throws an error" usually a weak property to check on its own?
choices: A function that always returns the wrong answer without throwing would pass it every time — it says nothing about whether the output is correct
JavaScript functions are technically incapable of throwing errors
It's not possible to write a generator for this property
It only applies to functions with no arguments
items.explanation: "Never throws" only catches crashes, not incorrect results — a function that silently returns wrong answers would still pass this check on every run.

items.prompt: What makes a property genuinely useful, rather than trivially true?
choices: It's a true, checkable invariant that says something about the actual output's correctness, not just that execution completed
It has to be checkable without running any code at all
It must be the shortest possible line of code
It has to mention every parameter the function accepts
items.explanation: A property earns its keep by actually constraining what a correct output can look like — properties that are always true regardless of correctness (like 'never throws' alone) barely test anything.

items.prompt: Per L2's flowchart, what happens immediately after a property check fails on a generated input?
choices: Shrinking begins: the tool tries smaller/simpler variants of the failing input to find the minimal reproducing case
The property is immediately reported as passing
The generator is deleted and a new one is written
The original function under test is automatically rewritten
items.explanation: A failure triggers shrinking, not an immediate report of the raw failing input — the tool spends extra effort minimizing the counterexample before reporting it.

items.prompt: Per L2's flowchart, if a property test runs its configured number of times with every run passing, what's the result?
choices: The property is treated as holding (a pass) — not proven for every possible input, but checked against far more cases than hand-written examples
The property is mathematically proven true for all inputs
The test is automatically re-run with double the number of cases forever
Shrinking runs anyway, just to double-check
items.explanation: All runs passing means the generator didn't find a counterexample in that many tries — strong evidence, not a mathematical proof that covers every possible input.

items.prompt: A property test runs 100 times and all 100 pass. Has this proven the property true for every possible input?
choices: No — it means the generator didn't happen to produce a failing case in those 100 tries; a rare edge case could still exist
Yes — 100 runs is mathematically sufficient to prove any property
Yes, but only if the function has fewer than 100 possible inputs
No — property tests can never provide any confidence at all
items.explanation: A property test is a strong automated search for a counterexample, not a proof — more runs raise confidence, they don't eliminate the possibility of a rare untested case.

items.prompt: Why might increasing the number of runs from 100 to 1000 be worth the extra time for a given property test?
choices: It increases the odds of hitting a rare failing case that a smaller number of runs might miss entirely
It guarantees the property is now mathematically proven
It makes the generator start producing only edge cases
It has no effect on the odds of finding a bug
items.explanation: More runs mean more chances for the generator to stumble onto whichever input(s) actually break the property — useful when a bug is rare, though never a guarantee of finding it.

items.prompt: Per L2, how is a generator for `{ name: string, age: number }` typically built?
choices: By composing a string generator and a number generator, mirroring how the type itself is built from those two fields
By hard-coding a fixed list of valid objects in advance
It cannot be generated automatically and must always be written by hand
By randomly generating raw bytes and hoping they parse as valid JSON
items.explanation: Generators compose the same way types do — a generator for an object type is built from generators for its fields, letting structured random values be produced automatically.

items.prompt: Why does generator composition matter for testing anything beyond primitive types like numbers and strings?
choices: It's what lets a property-testing library generate meaningfully-structured random objects, not just unstructured noise
It makes property tests run without needing a generator at all
It's only relevant for functions that don't accept any arguments
It removes the need to ever write a property
items.explanation: Without composition, generating realistic structured data (nested objects, arrays of records) by hand would be as tedious as writing examples by hand — composition is what makes generation scale to real-world shapes.

items.prompt: For an oracle-comparison property (comparing a fast custom sort against the built-in sort), why does the oracle implementation not need to be fast?
choices: The oracle only exists to check correctness during testing — its own performance is irrelevant since it never runs in production
A slow oracle makes the property test run faster overall
Oracle implementations are always faster than the code they check by definition
The oracle replaces the function under test entirely once testing is done
items.explanation: An oracle's only job is being obviously, verifiably correct — being slow is a completely acceptable trade-off since it's a testing tool, not the shipped implementation.

items.prompt: What has to be true about an oracle implementation for an oracle-comparison property to actually be useful?
choices: The oracle must itself be trustworthy/obviously correct — comparing against another buggy implementation proves nothing
The oracle must use the exact same algorithm as the function under test
The oracle must be written in a different programming language
The oracle must run faster than the function under test
items.explanation: An oracle-comparison property is only as strong as the oracle's own correctness — if the reference implementation itself has a bug, agreement between the two proves nothing about either one.

items.prompt: Complete checkRoundTrip(x) so it returns true exactly when decode(encode(x)) equals x, using JSON deep equality (JSON.stringify comparison is fine here since x only ever contains JSON-safe values).

tests.description: the property catches the empty-array bug (JSON.stringify([]) is not the empty string, but decode(encode(undefined)) breaks)

items.explanation: A round-trip property compares the doubly-transformed value back against the original, using deep equality rather than reference equality since encode/decode produces a structurally-equal but different object. `encode(undefined)` is `undefined` (JSON.stringify returns undefined, not a string), so `decode(encode(undefined))` calls decode(undefined), which does not match the empty-string branch and instead throws inside JSON.parse. A property check has to treat a thrown error as a failure too (hence the try/catch) — a real failure the property catches immediately, the same way L1's Scenario found the empty-array case.
items.reference:
🔁 round-trip: decode(encode(x)) should equal x, for any x
⚖️ deep equality is required — the two values are structurally equal, not the same reference

Why: a round-trip property is checkable without re-implementing encode/decode — it only needs to compare the input to the doubly-transformed output.

items.prompt: Complete checkRoundTrip(list) so it returns true exactly when reverse(reverse(list)) equals list, using JSON deep equality for the comparison.
items.explanation: Reversing twice is a round-trip: undoing the reversal by reversing again should always recover the original order, for any list including the empty one — a case that's trivial to skip when hand-writing examples.
items.reference:
🔁 round-trip: decode(encode(x)) should equal x, for any x
⚖️ deep equality is required — the two values are structurally equal, not the same reference

Why: a round-trip property is checkable without re-implementing encode/decode — it only needs to compare the input to the doubly-transformed output.

items.prompt: mergeIntervals should preserve the total set of integer points covered by the input. Complete coversSamePoints(intervals) so it returns true if the set of points covered by mergeIntervals(intervals) exactly matches the set of points covered by the raw input intervals.

tests.description: a contained interval exposes the bug: coverage is NOT preserved

items.explanation: The property compares the covered-points set before and after merging. On a contained interval like {1,10} and {2,3}, the buggy mergeIntervals sets last.end = curr.end (3), discarding points 4 through 10 — exactly the minimal counterexample L3's worked example shrinks down to.
items.reference:
📐 coverage-preserving: the set of points covered shouldn't change after merging
🐛 a contained interval (fully inside another) is the case 3 hand-picked examples missed

Why: stating the invariant directly (same coverage in and out) catches a bug that no small set of increasing-end examples would ever trigger.

items.prompt: Using the same buggy mergeIntervals and pointsCovered helpers, complete findsBug(intervals) so it returns true exactly when calling mergeIntervals on the given intervals loses at least one covered point compared to the raw input (i.e. the bug is triggered).

tests.description: a contained interval triggers the bug
non-overlapping intervals do not trigger the bug
increasing-end overlapping intervals do not trigger the bug

items.explanation: This checks specifically for lost coverage (points present before merging but missing after). The bug only loses points when a later interval is fully contained in the current merged range, since that's the only case where last.end = curr.end shrinks the range instead of extending or leaving it unchanged.
items.reference:
📐 coverage-preserving: the set of points covered shouldn't change after merging
🐛 a contained interval (fully inside another) is the case 3 hand-picked examples missed

Why: stating the invariant directly (same coverage in and out) catches a bug that no small set of increasing-end examples would ever trigger.

items.prompt: Complete shrinkByRemoval(items, stillFails) so it tries removing one item at a time from the array and returns the first smaller array for which stillFails(smallerArray) is true. If no removal still fails, return the original items unchanged.

tests.description: removes the one unnecessary item when a smaller failing array exists
returns the original array when no single removal still fails
finds the first removal that still fails, scanning from the start

items.explanation: This is the core move a shrinker makes: try the biggest available simplification (removing a whole element) and take the first one that still reproduces the failure. It's a single step of the loop L3 builds in full — real shrinkers repeat this kind of pass until nothing smaller still fails.
items.reference:
✂️ shrinking tries the biggest simplification first (remove a whole element)
🔁 repeats until no smaller variant still fails

Why: a minimal counterexample is far easier to debug than the first (possibly huge) random failure a generator finds.

items.prompt: Complete shrinkToMinimal(items, stillFails) so it repeatedly removes one item at a time (using the same single-removal idea) until no further single removal still fails, then returns the final array.

tests.description: shrinks down to just the two items that matter
shrinks down to a single required item
returns the original when nothing can be removed

items.explanation: This is the full loop, not just one pass: keep removing single items as long as some removal still reproduces the failure, and stop once none do. It's exactly L3's shrink() function, minus the bounds-tightening step — the repetition is what converges on a genuinely minimal case instead of stopping after the first successful removal.
items.reference:
✂️ shrinking tries the biggest simplification first (remove a whole element)
🔁 repeats until no smaller variant still fails

Why: a minimal counterexample is far easier to debug than the first (possibly huge) random failure a generator finds.

items.prompt: Per L3's trade-off table, why is `formatCurrency(4210)` → `"$42.10"` a poor candidate for property-based testing?
choices: There's no clean property simpler than the implementation itself — example tests are still the right tool here
Currency formatting functions cannot be tested at all
Property-based testing only works on functions that return arrays
The function has too many possible inputs to ever generate
items.explanation: Some functions genuinely don't have a clean invariant simpler than re-implementing the logic — for those, hand-picked example tests remain the more practical, more readable choice.

items.prompt: What's the practical lesson from L3's trade-off table about writing properties?
choices: Properties are harder to write than examples because you have to identify a true invariant, not just record one input/output pair — and not every function has one
Every function has an equally easy property to write, without exception
Properties should always be preferred over examples, with no exceptions
Writing a property is exactly as much work as writing one example test
items.explanation: Property-based testing has a real cost: finding a genuine invariant takes more thought than picking an input/output pair, and for some functions no clean property exists at all.

items.prompt: Per L3's Checkpoint, if genInterval only ever generated start < end (never start === end), what kind of bug becomes impossible to find?
choices: Any bug specific to zero-length intervals (start === end), since the generator would never produce that shape
Every possible bug in mergeIntervals
Only bugs involving negative numbers
No bugs are affected by this change
items.explanation: A property test's coverage is bounded by what its generator can actually produce — if start === end is never generated, no number of runs and no amount of shrinking can discover a bug that only shows up on that shape.

items.prompt: Per L3's trade-off table, what problem does a generator that's too broad cause, and what's the usual fix?
choices: It wastes runs on invalid inputs a real caller could never produce; the fix is a precondition filter that discards and re-generates invalid cases
It causes the function under test to throw a compile error
It makes shrinking impossible to perform
There is no real downside to a generator being too broad
items.explanation: A too-broad generator (e.g. producing intervals where start > end) spends runs on inputs a real caller couldn't produce, wasting effort — a precondition filter (like fast-check's fc.pre()) discards those and re-generates a valid one instead.

items.prompt: Per L3's trade-off table, a property test fails only 1 run in 500 and looks like flaky-tests' non-determinism. What's the recommended fix?
choices: Use a fixed random seed on failure, so the exact failing input reproduces deterministically instead of only 'sometimes'
Delete the property test since it can never be trusted
Ignore any failure that doesn't happen on every single run
Reduce the number of runs to 1 so failures are always consistent
items.explanation: The randomness is real, but the fix isn't to eliminate it — capturing the seed on a failing run makes that exact failing input reproducible on demand, turning an apparently-flaky failure into a deterministic, debuggable one.

items.prompt: Why does a rare, seed-dependent property-test failure look similar to the non-determinism `flaky-tests` describes, even though the underlying cause is different?
choices: Both present the same way to a developer — a test that sometimes passes and sometimes fails with no code change in between
They are actually the exact same problem with no meaningful difference at all
Property tests can never fail for any reason other than true flakiness
flaky-tests only applies to tests with no randomness involved
items.explanation: On the surface both look identical (inconsistent pass/fail with unchanged code), which is why the same discipline applies: pin down exactly what varied between runs — here, the random seed — rather than shrugging it off as flakiness.

items.prompt: In fast-check's actual API, what does fc.pre(condition) do inside a property function?
choices: Discards the current generated input and re-generates a new one when the condition is false, acting as a precondition filter
Deletes the property test entirely
Automatically fixes the input so the condition becomes true
Runs the property function twice in a row
items.explanation: fc.pre() is fast-check's real precondition mechanism — when the condition is false for a generated input, that run is discarded and a fresh input is generated, keeping every actual check meaningful.

items.prompt: In fast-check's actual API, what happens by default when fc.assert(fc.property(...)) finds a failing case?
choices: It automatically shrinks the failure and reports the minimal counterexample
It silently ignores the failure and reports a pass
It immediately stops the entire test process with no information
It requires the developer to manually write a shrinking function first
items.explanation: fast-check bundles generation, running, and shrinking together — a failure triggers automatic shrinking to a minimal counterexample as part of the same fc.assert() call, with no extra code required from the author.
